subtype: Approach: asking a parent to hold the device [Action]
passage: Emil had noticed something: once the tablet was in his hand, homework stopped. On Sunday evening in their Oslo flat he carried it to the kitchen. "Mamma, can you keep this from four to six? I will ask for it back after." His mother raised her eyebrows. "Whose idea is this?" "Mine. I cannot stop once I start." She slid it into the drawer with the spare keys. At four Emil opened his reader, and his eyes strayed to the drawer only twice. His little brother Diego asked for a turn with it, and Mamma said no. At six Emil got the tablet back, homework done, and played without a worry.

qa.q: Where did Emil's mother put the tablet?
qa.a: She put it in the drawer with the spare keys.

qa.q: What did Emil realise about himself, and what did he want as a result?
qa.a: He realised he could not stop once he started, so he wanted his mother's help to stay on track, and he chose it himself.

qa.q: What could Emil do if his mother is away one evening?
qa.a: He could put the tablet in another room himself and set a timer, because distance and a limit still help when she is not there.

qa.q: How might Mamma feel when Emil asks for this himself?
qa.a: Probably surprised and proud, since she asked whose idea it was and he answered that it was his. 🙂

grounding: A boy who finds it hard to stop asks his mother to hold the tablet during study hours, a limit he chose himself.

subtopic: Telling the truth after a mistake
passage: Sunday night. Today my cricket shot smashed Aparna Aunty's kitchen window. Crash! Everyone scattered, but I stayed by the wall with my heart thumping. I thought about running home. Then I thought that would be worse. I told Papa in one breath. He said, "Come, we will go together." At her door my voice shook: "Aunty, it was my ball. I am sorry. I can give my pocket money for the glass." She looked at the window, then at me, and said, "Thank you for coming yourself. Nobody was hurt, and that is what matters." Papa is paying the glass mender and I will give him my savings every week. I expected shouting. I got a laddoo. Jagdish

qa.q: What did Aparna Aunty give Jagdish?
qa.a: She gave Jagdish a laddoo.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling while standing by the wall after the crash?
qa.a: Frightened, since Jagdish's heart was thumping and running home crossed Jagdish's mind.

qa.q: What could Jagdish do to make the repair fairer?
qa.a: Give weekly savings towards the glass or offer to help Aunty with small jobs, because repair shows care beyond words.

qa.q: How might Aparna Aunty feel when Jagdish came to her door?
qa.a: Probably surprised and touched, since she thanked Jagdish for coming in person and said nobody was hurt.

grounding: Jagdish owns up straight away after breaking a window, goes to the door with Papa and offers to help pay.

subtopic: Telling the truth after a mistake
subtype: Approach: imagining the consequences of each choice [Thinking]
passage: The blue ink had made a dark flower on the cream sofa, and Parveen's pen lay in her lap. She could slide a cushion over it. She pictured tomorrow: Mummy finds it, asks, and I say I do not know. Then Mummy remembers I was the only one here. That would make her angrier, and she would not believe me next time. If I tell her now, there will be a scolding, for sure. But she will still trust me tomorrow. Parveen breathed in and went to the kitchen, where her mother Sarita was chopping onions. "Mummy, I got ink all over the sofa." Sarita put the knife down and sighed. "Show me." Her voice was sharp, but she held Parveen's hand.

qa.q: What did Parveen spill on the sofa?
qa.a: Parveen spilled blue ink on the cream sofa.

qa.q: What was Parveen worried about if she hid the ink?
qa.a: That the lie would be found, her mother would be angrier, and she would not be believed next time.

qa.q: What could Parveen offer after telling the truth?
qa.a: She could ask how to help fix the stain with her mother's guidance, because helping shows she takes responsibility.

qa.q: How might Sarita feel about being told straight away?
qa.a: Annoyed about the sofa but glad of the honesty, since her voice was sharp yet she held Parveen's hand.

grounding: A girl weighs that a lie may be found and cost her mother's trust, while the truth costs a scolding now.

subtopic: Telling the truth after a mistake
subtype: Approach: blaming a sibling or the dog [Pitfall]
passage: Thursday. I broke Amma's blue vase with the football. Amma came running and I said, "Meenu did it." Meenu, my little sister, is five. She cried and said no, and I said she had been standing right there. Amma gave her a long scolding and no dessert. Meenu looked at me with her wet face and I could not look back. Then Amma asked why Meenu was lying, and I said a third thing that was not true, that Meenu had touched it before. Three lies in one evening. My stomach feels sick. Every time I think it is over, I need one more story to hold it up. I keep thinking I should tell Amma. Kishore

qa.q: How old is Meenu?
qa.a: Meenu, my little sister, is five.

qa.q: What is Kishore feeling as Meenu is scolded?
qa.a: Guilty and sick, since Kishore watched Meenu take the blame and could not look back.

qa.q: What could Kishore do to fix this?
qa.a: Tell Amma the truth and say sorry to Meenu, because the lie keeps needing more lies and Meenu is paying for it.

qa.q: How does the evening feel to Meenu?
qa.a: Unfair and upsetting, since Meenu cried, was scolded and lost dessert for something Meenu did not do.

grounding: Kishore blames a little sister for a broken vase, feels awful, and needs more lies to hold the first one up.

subtopic: Telling the truth after a mistake
passage: The closing bell would ring in five minutes, and Chetan's borrowed adventure book had a long tear across page forty. He pushed it behind a row of atlases on the low shelf and hurried out, hoping nobody would look. At home dinner tasted like paper. In class he kept glancing at the door as if Anjali Ma'am might walk in. On Thursday the librarian pulled the book from the shelf, found the tear, checked the card and came to Chetan's desk at recess. "This one was yours, I think?" she asked gently. His ears burned. He had carried the worry for four days, and hearing it out loud felt, oddly, lighter.

qa.q: Where did Chetan hide the book?
qa.a: He hid it behind a row of atlases on the low shelf.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling in the days after hiding the book?
qa.a: Anxious, since dinner tasted like paper and he kept glancing at the door.

qa.q: What could Chetan have done at the shelf instead, and why?
qa.a: He could have told the librarian about the tear at once, because a torn page can be mended and the worry would have been avoided.

qa.q: How might Anjali Ma'am see the torn book and Chetan?
qa.a: As a repairable accident, since she asked gently instead of scolding, which suggests she cares more about the truth than about punishing.

grounding: A boy who tore a library book hides it behind other books, and the secret makes him anxious until the librarian asks.

subtopic: Telling the truth after a mistake
subtype: Approach: preparing the words before confessing [Thinking]
passage: Zanele rehearsed on the school bus in Durban, moving her lips. First: say it plainly, I lost your pencil box. Second: say sorry, and mean it. Third: offer to replace it from my pocket money. She practised until the words stopped shaking. At the gate she found her friend Hiroshi kicking a stone, hands in his pockets. "Hiroshi, I lost your pencil box yesterday. I am really sorry. I will buy you a new one with my pocket money." Hiroshi's face fell, then he shrugged. "It was a gift from my grandfather, but thank you for telling me." Zanele swallowed. She had not planned for that. "I will look again in the classroom too," she said.

qa.q: What three things did Zanele plan to say?
qa.a: She planned to say she lost the pencil box, say sorry and offer to replace it from her pocket money.

qa.q: What was Zanele feeling on the bus while she rehearsed?
qa.a: Nervous, since she moved her lips until the words stopped shaking. 😅

qa.q: What else could Zanele do after apologising?
qa.a: Search the classroom and the lost-property box with Hiroshi, because finding the box would mean more than a replacement.

qa.q: How might Hiroshi feel about the lost pencil box and the apology?
qa.a: Sad about the gift but appreciative of the honesty, since his face fell and then he thanked Zanele for telling him.

grounding: A girl who lost a friend's pencil box rehearses admitting it, saying sorry and offering to replace it.

subtopic: Telling the truth after a mistake
subtype: Approach: confessing late after first lying [Revision]
passage: After dinner Rafael said, "Mama, my homework is done," and went to watch cartoons. But the words followed him around the room like a stray dog. The cartoons stopped being funny. At half past eight he stood at the door of Lindiwe's bedroom with his reading book behind his back. "Mama, I lied. I have not done the reading or the spelling." His mother put down her knitting. "Thank you for telling me. I am not happy about the lie, but I am glad you came. Now get your book. Twenty minutes tonight, and the rest tomorrow." Rafael felt lighter, even holding the book.

qa.q: What did Rafael say he had not done?
qa.a: He said he had not done the reading or the spelling.

qa.q: How did Rafael feel after saying his homework was done?
qa.a: Guilty, because the words followed him around the room and spoiled the cartoons.

qa.q: What could Rafael do in future to avoid the same trap?
qa.a: Say honestly how much is left and ask for time, because telling the truth first avoids the guilt.

qa.q: How might Lindiwe feel about the confession?
qa.a: Displeased about the lie but glad that he came, since she thanked him and still asked him to finish the work.

grounding: A boy lies about homework, feels bad all evening, confesses before bed, and his mother thanks him but still expects the work.

subtopic: Telling the truth after a mistake
subtype: Approach: fixing the harm along with the apology [Action]
passage: My name is Kashish, and this is about the day I spilled water on Zubin's drawing of a lighthouse. He had worked on it for a week. The blue sea ran into the sky. I said sorry right away, and Zubin nodded, but sorry did not bring the lighthouse back. So after school I asked to borrow the pencil sketch, and I redrew the lighthouse slowly on a clean sheet, following his outline. It took two evenings, and mine leaned a little. When I gave it back Zubin looked at it for a long time and said, "It leans. But thanks." I still think that was the right thing to do.

qa.q: What did Kashish spill on Zubin's drawing?
qa.a: Kashish spilled water on it.

qa.q: What did Kashish feel about saying sorry alone?
qa.a: Kashish felt it did not fix the loss and wanted to make it right, so the lighthouse was redrawn.

qa.q: What could Kashish do if the second drawing still disappoints Zubin?
qa.a: Ask what would help and offer to redo the coloured parts together, because repair means listening to the person who lost the work.

qa.q: How might Zubin see the redrawn lighthouse?
qa.a: As a kind effort even though it leans, since Zubin looked at it a long time and said thanks.

grounding: Kashish says sorry and also redraws the spoiled drawing, so repair goes beyond words.

subtopic: Telling the truth after a mistake
passage: "Where were you?" Danish's mother, Preeti, asked as the door opened. "At the park," said Danish. "With Sohail. We played cricket." "The park is fine. Which way did you come back?" Danish looked at his shoes. "The usual way." "The usual way, or through the market road?" No answer. "Danish. I told you the market road has trucks." "I told you the truth! I was at the park." Preeti sat down slowly. "You told me the truth about the park and left out the part that matters. That is still hiding something." Danish's ears turned pink. "Next time tell me the whole thing," she said, "and we will find a safe way to go together."

qa.q: Which road had Preeti told Danish to avoid?
qa.a: She had told him to avoid the market road.

qa.q: What did Danish believe about what he told his mother?
qa.a: He believed it was fine because what he said about the park was true, though looking at his shoes suggests some unease about the road.

qa.q: What could Danish have said, and why would it help?
qa.a: He could have told the whole route, including the market road, and asked for a safe way, because his mother could then help with the risk.

qa.q: How might Preeti feel about the half-truth?
qa.a: Worried about the trucks and hurt that the important part was left out, since she said it was still hiding something.

grounding: A boy tells only the park part of his outing and leaves out the road he was told to avoid, so the risk stays hidden from his mother.

subtopic: Telling the truth after a mistake
subtype: Approach: asking a trusted elder for help in confessing [Action]
passage: I am Nazia, and I was on the stairs of our building when I saw Bilal from the second floor sitting on a step with a folded test paper. His sister Zainab came up and sat beside him. I heard only pieces: "Papa will shout." "I will come with you. You tell it, and I will help." They went in together. Later Zainab told me over the railing that Papa, their father, had gone quiet, then asked what the plan was, and the plan was that she would go over the fractions with Bilal every evening. When Bilal came out he was pale but standing straighter. I could not tell if he was relieved or only tired.

qa.q: What was Bilal holding while he sat on the stairs?
qa.a: Bilal was holding a folded test paper.

qa.q: How might Bilal have felt on the step, according to Nazia?
qa.a: Afraid of his father's reaction, since Nazia overheard "Papa will shout" and saw him holding the paper, though Nazia can only guess.

qa.q: What could Bilal do next to follow the plan?
qa.a: Go over the fractions with Zainab each evening and show progress, because it gives their father concrete steps to see.

qa.q: How might Zainab see her brother's fear?
qa.a: As something she could ease, since she sat with him, offered to go in with him and helped make a plan.

grounding: A boy afraid of his father's anger over a low mark first tells his older sister, who goes with him and helps him plan to improve.
